Confidence-Ordering Reversal under Contextual Priors in Neural Decoding

Anonymous Authors

Anonymous submission, under review

Paper (coming soon) Code BibTeX
TL;DR Contextual priors can make neural decoding errors more confident: the fused margin ranks repairs above residual errors near the top of the local ranking but below them further down; keeping local and prior scores separate recovers the ordering.

Abstract

Contextual priors improve neural-to-language decoding by reshaping candidate scores. However, confidence is read from the same reshaped scores, so the errors a prior leaves behind can become more confident with no change in accuracy to reveal it. In this work, we ask how a prior shapes the confidence of these errors, studying speech retrieval on MEG-MASC and MOUS with local decoding scores and a contextual prior combined by additive shallow fusion, and the fused top-two margin as confidence. Among initially incorrect predictions, we find a confidence-ordering reversal: a larger margin makes a repair, an error that fusion corrects, more likely when the correct candidate starts near the top of the local ranking, but less likely when it starts lower. On MEG-MASC, pooled correctness AUROC is 0.87, yet the AUROC separating repairs from residual errors, which fusion leaves uncorrected, falls from 0.70 at initial ranks 2–3 to 0.39 at ranks 21–50. Errors starting beyond rank 20, inside the reversed region, make up 46.6% of all errors after fusion. We propose a score-level account: a repair must first close the correct candidate's initial deficit, which limits its final margin, whereas a residual error can build a large margin between two incorrect candidates. Through a causal intervention that changes only the fusion weight, we show that the reversal moves to deeper ranks, as the account predicts, and that under a word-level LM prior it keeps moving after accuracy gain peaks, so a weight chosen for accuracy does not settle confidence. Guided by this account, we read local and prior scores separately: read before fusion, the prior's own scores already separate repairs from residual errors where the fused margin reverses, and estimators built on local and prior scores let a selective decoder answer on 74.5% of windows instead of 56.7%, with 92% of its output sets still containing the correct candidate. Confidence after contextual fusion should retain the local and contextual evidence behind each prediction, not just the fused scores.

The fused margin reverses its ordering across initial ranks

We study offline speech retrieval, keeping a fixed candidate pool and separate local and prior scores. The fused margin, the gap between the two highest fused scores, serves as confidence. Among initially incorrect predictions, repairs become correct after fusion and residual errors remain incorrect. We group these errors by the correct candidate's initial rank under the local scores.

Near the top of the local ranking, larger margins favour repairs: from the smallest to largest margin quartile, the repair rate rises from 42.4% to 84.4% at ranks 2–3. Further down, larger margins favour residual errors: at ranks 21–50 it falls from 1.37% to 0.55%. The pre-fusion margin favours residual errors in every group, so the positive ordering near the top is produced by fusion itself. The reversal replicates on MOUS, at the participant level, within sentences, and for entropy and other summaries of the fused scores.

Why: how repairs and residual errors form their margins

With local scores s, prior scores π, and fusion weight α, additive fusion gives s̃ = s + απ. Let G0 be the correct candidate's initial score deficit and Δπ the prior score range. On a repair, comparison with the strongest local competitor gives

G0 ≤ αΔπ,     m(s̃) ≤ αΔπ − G0.

A repair must first close the deficit, so the larger the deficit, the less room remains for its final margin. A residual error has no such limit: deep in the ranking, its margin mostly compares two incorrect candidates. The correct candidate is the fused runner-up in 75.2% of residual errors at ranks 2–3 but only 2.1% at ranks 21–50, so the prior can widen the gap between wrong candidates even while it moves the right one up. Because the bound follows from additive fusion itself, it predicts that increasing the fusion weight extends positive ordering towards larger initial deficits.

A causal intervention on the fusion weight

We vary only the fusion weight, keeping local and prior scores fixed, and recompute outcomes at every weight. Under the history-aggregation prior, positive ordering extends from no rank group to ranks 11–20 and to larger score deficits, and the boundary never retreats in any of 1,000 participant-bootstrap resamples.

Under a word-level teacher-forced LM prior, positive ordering keeps expanding after accuracy gain peaks: validation selects α = 0.5 for accuracy (+11.20 points, positive ordering through ranks 6–10), while at α = 1 the gain falls to +9.16 points and positive ordering reaches every observed group through rank 100. Accuracy and confidence ordering are two different responses to the same prior, so a weight chosen for accuracy does not settle confidence.

Reading local and prior scores separately

Fusion merges local competition and prior support into one margin. Read before fusion, the prior's own margin separates the outcomes that the fused margin reverses: under history aggregation it reaches 0.937 at ranks 21–50, against 0.392 for the fused margin, and stays above 0.7 in all 32 cells of the fusion-weight sweep. Learned estimators built on local and prior scores rank repairs above residual errors where the fused margin reverses (0.910 at ranks 21–50 with prior features).

These scores also let a selective decoder answer more often at the same coverage. At matched 92.24% coverage, emission rises from the fused margin through richer fused-score features to local and prior features:

Fused margintop-two gap of fused scores156.76.3
Fused scoresfused gaps at K = 1–20, entropy666.65.8
Decoder scores+ local margin and entropy872.55.2
Full+ prior features1574.55.2

Recalibrating the fused margin cannot do this: any strictly increasing recalibration preserves its ordering, so no calibration can undo the reversal.

Takeaway

A contextual prior sets both which prediction wins and how confident its errors look. Pooled confidence metrics can stay high while the ordering reverses exactly where remaining errors concentrate. Confidence estimation after contextual fusion should therefore keep the local evidence and contextual support behind each prediction, rather than any summary of the fused scores alone.
